items.title: Terri Lyne Carrington interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003
items.q: And to me Elvin and Roy are two of my favorite drummers. ... But anyway Roy plays like with this kind of motion.

ctx.x: Let me ask you about this concept about playing ahead or behind the beat. Is there such a thing as that or is it something that people that write about music invented?

Well there’s definitely such a thing. To be critical of it is, I find that some people are very staunch about — I can’t tell you if somebody plays behind the beat oh my God. There’s a lot of people that feel like that. There’s a lot of people that feel like rushing is such a © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -13-

horrible thing or playing on top of the beat. For me I think that it goes beyond that. I try to look at it if you are a strong musician the beat can be elastic. Sometimes I purposely pull the beat back. Sometimes I purposely push it forward. But I had to become strong as a drummer, strong with my concepts and strong with well basically my convictions about music to be able to be comfortable doing that. Because sometimes you get into whatever the tempo is and you feel as a drummer you have to lock something into…

items.title: Roy Haynes — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: She studied with Alan a while. What do you think? That we sounded similar or something?

ctx.x: Terri Lyne. She studied with Alan a while. What do you think? That we sounded similar or something? Well, Alan sounded similar, and then maybe Tony at first, a long time ago. But other than that, who else do you think has that Boston sound you’re talking about?
Just – I would say you three, primarily.
